### How to insert a node while keeping a linked list sorted

Below is a concise, working C implementation that inserts a new integer into a singly‑linked list **in ascending order**.  
The code follows the logic described in the lecture notes (see source [1]).

```c
#include <cs50.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

typedef struct node
{
    int number;          // the value stored in this node
    struct node *next;   // pointer to the next node (or NULL)
} node;

/* Insert a new node with value `number` into the list so that the list stays sorted. */
void insert_sorted(node **head, int number)
{
    /* Allocate the new node */
    node *n = malloc(sizeof(node));
    if (n == NULL)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        exit(1);
    }
    n->number = number;
    n->next = NULL;

    /* 1. Empty list – the new node becomes the head. */
    if (*head == NULL)
    {
        *head = n;
        return;
    }

    /* 2. New number is smaller than the first element – prepend. */
    if (number < (*head)->number)
    {
        n->next = *head;   // point new node to current head
        *head = n;         // new node becomes new head
        return;
    }

    /* 3. Otherwise, walk the list until we find the insertion point. */
    node *prev = *head;
    node *curr = (*head)->next;

    while (curr != NULL && curr->number < number)
    {
        prev = curr;
        curr = curr->next;
    }

    /* 4. Insert between prev and curr.
       - If curr is NULL, we are at the end and the new node becomes the last node.
       - If curr is not NULL, we insert before curr. */
    n->next = curr;
    prev->next = n;
}
```

#### What the code does in each scenario

| Scenario | What the code checks / does | Why it works |
|----------|----------------------------|--------------|
| **List is empty** | `if (*head == NULL)` | The new node is the only element, so it becomes the head. |
| **New number < first element** | `if (number < (*head)->number)` | The new node must be placed before the current head. We set its `next` to the old head and update the head pointer. |
| **New number > all existing elements** | The `while` loop runs until `curr == NULL`. | `prev` ends up pointing to the last node. We set `prev->next` to the new node, and the new node’s `next` stays `NULL`. |
| **New number falls somewhere in the middle** | The `while` loop stops when `curr->number >= number`. | `prev` points to the node after which the new node should be inserted, and `curr` is the node that will come after the new node. We splice the new node between them (`prev->next = n; n->next = curr`). |

#### Why the logic changes

* **Empty list** – no traversal needed; just set the head.
* **Smaller than first element** – we can insert at the very front without walking the list; this is a constant‑time operation.
* **Larger than all elements** – we must walk to the end of the list (O(n) time) because we don’t know where the end is until we reach a node whose `next` is `NULL`.
* **Middle insertion** – we walk until we find the first node whose value is **not** smaller than the new number. The new node is inserted just before that node. This also requires a linear scan in the worst case.

The overall time complexity of `insert_sorted` is **O(n)**, where *n* is the number of nodes already in the list, because in the worst case we may have to traverse the entire list to find the correct spot. However, the constant‑time cases (empty list or new smallest element) are handled efficiently.
